title: Whoever Is Hungry
logline: Every evening one person feeds the same stray dogs by name and checks their wounds, while passers-by toss them scraps to watch them scramble.

object.note: Object 2 (identity not chosen) may appear subtly, for example among Chathura's things while he travels, waits or watches, only where it sits naturally in a real moment. Never staged, never the subject.

thread_in.thread: The question of wanting to be seen passes from what people wear to what they give: an evening gathering place where the same stray dogs are fed for very different reasons.

thread_out.thread: From the pleasure of watching something eat to the pleasure of watching something fly: on the southern coast in the windy season, a kite and the wish for it to be seen.

requirements: A public place with a consistent stray-dog population and a known regular feeder
Consent from the feeder to be followed over several evenings
Passers-by willing to be filmed in an ordinary public space

suggestions.name: A bus stand or temple compound in Kandy town
suggestions.why: A well-known town centre with public gathering places where stray animals are commonly present.
suggestions.verify: No feeder has been identified or contacted; this is a plausible setting only.

unknowns: No participant, access or event has been found or confirmed.

lesson.in_simple_terms: Feeding a hungry dog can be about the dog, or about the fun of watching it scramble. The texts count the first as kindness and the second as a kind of wanting, even though the hand does the same thing.
lesson.in_simple_terms_si: බල්ලෙකුට කෑම දීම ඌ කෙරෙහි කරුණාවෙන් කළ හැකි අතර, ඌ කන හැටි බලා විනෝද වීමට ද කළ හැකිය; අත කරන දේ එකම වුවත් සිත වෙනස්ය.
lesson.the_teaching: The Abhidhamma gives this very example: feeding animals in order to enjoy watching them eat is counted among the greed-rooted minds, while feeding them as a kindness to them is counted as a wholesome mind (kusala citta). The texts also teach that the occasional mental factors, including effort and desire-to-act (chanda), are not good or bad in themselves but take on the quality of the mind they join. Desire-to-act is the wish to do something, without the sticking that makes it greed.
lesson.how_the_film_shows_it: The regular feeder's bowls, the dogs' names and the checked wounds are set beside passers-by tossing scraps to watch a scramble, while the dogs eat the same food either way. The film never says which gesture is which; the viewer sees where each person's attention rests, on the dog or on the show.

key_terms.en: desire-to-act, wish to take up or do

lesson.caution: This does not mean that the passers-by are bad people or that enjoying animals is a sin; the texts describe moments of mind, and the film judges no one on screen.
lesson.builds_on: The last film found wanting in the aim behind the same garment; here the same line runs through an act of giving, and the film adds that the steady wish to do something is not itself greed.
lesson.evidence_class: editorial interpretation grounded in cited source teaching
